OK, so I'm labelling the RBD/DBR/RBR/DBD as Xa, and the reactions as Xb, c, d, etc.

Looking at the M5 (I don't have M1 data back here) we can see that 1a, 2a and 3a are all retests of DPs to go lower (1a DP is from the H1) and are thus FTRs in their own right. 2a, however does not have the significance of the other two, as it is a retest of a minor level.

1a. The internal structure is a bit messy, but as the move away is definite and prolonged, it maintains its significance. The fact it's a good FTR and a break of a flag says to pay attention on the First Time Back. In fact, the more I think about this one, the more it seems that it works because it's an FTR after breaking the three cirlces areas to the left. The lower is a nice flag limit. There is strong move away from level 1a in the end, though.

I can get tied up in knots with this, though, as every candle is an FTR to something!!

2a. This one is a bit choppy, and not such a definite move away. It is more of a reaction to what's going on in 1a than a fresh zone itself, and this is reflected in the weaker reaction at 2b.

3a. This is a nice, clean bit of PA. A strong move down which engulfs the low to the left, retests this break, and a second strong move down.

1b. The reaction is a nice rejection on the H1, but down on the M5 you can see what is likely an M1 QM. Even on the M5 there is a nice bear engulf, followed by a retest.

2b. The reaction is something I have seen a lot - first price bounces off the decision point to go lower, back at 2a, then moves up into the zone itself. It may be worth have one position at the DP, and a second if it returns into the zone. Needs investigating. Probably simpler just to have one at the low of the zone (that DP) unless the zone is a particularly wide one.

3b. The reaction has a couple of good, strong bear engulfs, and a nice rejection after these.

A stop above the zone would have worked in each case.

I would like to have these comments on charts, but MT4 is horrid, and takes ages, and everything else is clunky, too. Would anyone mind me doing this via video posts? It takes me 20 x as long to mark these up and write this, as it does to find the zones and reactions. These 3 have taken me several hours to write up.

Ok, so 4a is actually the reaction to 3a, so is not to be trusted, as it is not a fresh level, and it does fail over to the right. However, the first reaction isn't into the meat of the zone, it's at the DP to go lower, at 4a. This is shown by the red line. The ultimate high at 4b is into a discrete but strong move down that I wouldn't have spotted, but is a flip level, when looking left.

Similar to 1a from the previous post, there is a break of a flag creating the FTR shown which then has a decent reaction, shown in the insert. So this zone did work prior to the fail, but the best (easiest) opportunity for gain would be an entry at the bottom of the H1 zone, with a stop above. That's a big, fat zone, though, and the M5 allows it to be broken into distinct entry levels.

My logic from 1a does not work on the FTR in 4a, however, but 4a is operating over a smaller scale, and is not from such an extreme in price.

5, out of 200. 200? Really? Coooome ooooon.... seriously?

So, what I see here is that once again price has tested the decision point, shown as x, before then moving into the main part of the zone, shown as y. Now, the thing is, that x is the FTR of RBD that is 5a. So, this means we should expect a reaction on the return? Well, there isn't one, and the reaction actaully happens at y.

What this means for trying to trade these, is that the stop needs to go above the RBD high, unless there is some way to be sure which of these features is going to cause the reversal/reaction. Maybe the story shall unfold as we go further....

6a: DBR

So, we mark in the DBR at 6a, and wait to see what happens. As noted for 5, there is compression down into x (which is a DBR itself) and price has compressed away from x, making some stacked demand, so we shouldn't be surprised to see price move lower and reverse at 6b.

The engulf of 5a tells us that the path to go up is cleared, as 5a is a broken flag limit (I noted the pole earlier). So much easier in hindsight, though.

Now, once again, x is the FTR to 6a.

It's easy to see a pattern emerging, and I'm only at number 6!!!

It's maybe dangerous to go looking for PA in such a tight area, but the M5 shown that price CP'd away from 6a, and the only fresh demand was right at the extreme, which has the looks of a QM about it, too.

The reaction on the M5 is a strong move into the zone, with a small reaction, followed by a fake out, and a bullish engulf. Then, we have what looks like a QM. I'm starting to appreciate the importance of the fresh zone.

7a: RBD

This is interesting, as it shows why moving your stop to BE is a bad idea, and can take you out of a winning trade, especially if you go short at 7b, the retest of the DP to break the highs of the RBD (this will be a flag on a LTF). The drop from the high of 7a made a decent engulf, so a target at least back down to that engulf, around 'x' would be reasonable. That's only about a 1:1 RRR, though.

What I'm learning is that now the DP has been tested, we should watch for shorting opportunities higher into the zone. This setup is also suggesting to me that the retest of the DP (which is 7b) is only likely to be a decent FTR if price has dropped through some strong levels before it returns up to the FTR (I know this is a central teaching of RTM, but this is me now seeing why for myself). If it does not do this, and makes a move back up towards the FTR/meat of the zone, then we should expect price to engulf the FTR upwards, and then turn deeper into the zone. This is another reason the stop should remain above the xone and not be moved to BE until something major is engulfed to the downside.

Also, to the left I have marked some 'kind of' compression. There is some fresh demand in there which 7a and 7b have to fight through, but once price moves up to 7c, it's a clearer path down.

Note the compression leading up to 7b and the LQ/FO sucking in the breakout traders to go long. A consolidation below a level suggests that the level will be broken, so it's important to be able to differentiate CP from simple flat price oscillation (that's what a base is, I guess) and a sinking bull flag or you may be going short at a developing RBR, not an imminent drop. So, we want to see HHs and HLs as we approach a supply zone, if price looks like it's ranging below the zone.

The Blue line at 7a shows the extreme high of the reaction at 7c. When price gets up to 7c, it has already tested the H1 DP to move down at 7a, so we should "expect" it to now move deeper into the zone, and as it has made some nice engulfs downwards, and been away for some time, we can "expect" to now have a more substantial reaction. But where? Well, the extreme high seems to go to the edge of a CP PAZ at 7a (but I haven't focussed on those, yet) but easier to spot is the QM it has made at 7c. The red circle shows why you don't trail your stop near BE, and in fact, you may want to place a short right there.

8a: DBR

This one is messy, but that's no excuse to skip over it. If it's messy, we need to drop down a time frame or two, and now we can see that price has hung around in there for some time, and not made a truly convincing exit from the zone.

There's a lot going on in there, which is maybe a reason in itself to leave this zone alone.

The reaction at 8b comes at the DP/flip to the left, marked with the red line, and so looks like a fakeout of zone x, so I guess it pays to be aware of potential flips for stop placement.

Depending on trade management, you may have got away with this, but is it worth the effort when you can find some cleaner RBD/DBRs all over the place?

8c reacts to something I can't see with my data, but is one of the obvious areas of stronger demand. If you didn't TT this, you would have lost on this one. You would have been taking a TT at a level of stacked demand, which is balsy.

One final point, and another "driving the point home" lesson for me, is that the low marked "Tested, so expect deeper into zone" is the FTR for this H1 zone, despite how tiny it is. It does have a tiny reaction at 'z', but does not give the big move up one would like. Notice that price CP'd away from this FTR, it did not LQ away, so we should not take the First Time Back.

9a: RBD

I'm getting more info onto the H1 chart, now that I'm getting things a bit straighter in my head, and can be more concise. That's got to be a good thing.

In this case, the FTR created by the RBD that is 9a has a very strong move away, making it a good candidate for a FTB short, but where should we expect the short to happen? We need to look at the LTF to have an idea, but we can see on the H1 that the DP to go lower has already been tested, this is clearer on the M5, though.

Once more, the the test of the DP to go lower is an FTR in its own right, but right now, I'm picking my FTRs from the H1, and using the M5 for entries. If I pick FTRs off the M5, they are likely to be killed by the H1 action (or at least, it seems that way).

So, looking at 9a on the M5 I can see that the top is stacked supply, which is bad news. However, this looks like a good FTR/RBD on the H1, so it's a-ok to short it, as that must be considered the leading TF. But, as with DBR 8a from my previous example, the CP suggests to expect a reversal at the extreme of the zone. As I go through this homework, the validity of this logic shall prove true, or fail.

In the case of 9b we get the fantastic combo of some CP into the zone and a LQ spike right to the top edge of the zone, which forms a near perfect pin bar. Ooh, that's sexy.

Last thing. On the H1, looking at the big bull candle to the right of 9b, one might expect to see a reaction when price returns to the 9b level, as it looks like ignored supply, that shall become demand, yet that doesn't happen. My first thought was "Well, that would have been a failed trade". No, though, it's not ignored supply, as the supply has been removed by the 3 visits to the supply level, before dropping to the "obvious target" for 9b, so we should not expect price to "see" that level as it passes.

10: DBR

This one doesn't have the strongest move away from the base, and the decision to break upwards at x is not convincing. The break at y is a much stronger decision, making 11 the better prospect. But anyway, looking at 10a, I would like to see price move away more from x, then a return to test, as with the other decisions looked at so far, and this has not happened. Perhaps it is a contributing factor to price cutting right through the zone, at the return marked 10b.

Before price gets to 10b it makes a huge move down, completely ingoring the flag limit shown, so that has just GOT to be a target for any longs, and a great shorting op, too.

On the M5, the move away from 10a is messy, and partly compressed, and price hangs about in the zone for a while, which is not a good thing. If anywhere, we sould look for entries right at the extreme, as it looks like decent demand.

Interestingly, when we get to the reaction, at 10b, price cuts straight through the zone, but does not close below it on the M5. There is a fakeout into a demand area from a long time ago. I'm sure a limit order would have been stoped out, but price action did give a reason to enter.
